Case file · Pelston, Mary Eveline — Prime 2 Burkesville, Kentucky → North Riverside, Illinois · 1926–2014 · Status: known first-hand; paper trail still catching up

Mary Pelston
— the grandmother I knew

Mary Eveline Pelston was born in Cumberland County, Kentucky, in 1926, married Edward Joseph Dedo in Chicago in 1944, and spent most of her life in North Riverside, Illinois, as the grandmother her grandson Brent grew up knowing. This page walks her whole life — the Kentucky childhood, the census trail, two marriages, the house on 24th Street — and marks every load-bearing claim with what the evidence will actually carry: proven, probable, or still open. She is one of the few people in this family file who was known in person. The paper trail is thinner than the life, and the page says so wherever that is true.

§1 The woman

Most pages in this family file are built out of records alone. Mary's is not. Her grandson knew her — visited her house, heard her tell her own stories — and that first-hand knowledge is itself evidence, graded as such wherever it carries weight.

Her full name was Mary Eveline Pelston. The middle name rests on the strongest authority this file has for anything about her: Brent's own knowledge of his grandmother, confirmed in his words on 24 September 2026 — "Mary's middle name is Eveline; he personally knew his grandmother." Proven The records agree in their shorthand way: her 2014 obituary and the 1950 census both give her as "Mary E.," the 1940 census writes her "Evelyn," and her siblings' obituaries call her "Eveline" and "Evelyn" in turn. A family note that says "Mary Elizabeth Pelston" belongs to a different woman — a Mary born in 1905 who died in 1990 — and is not merged with this one. Disproven as an identity for Brent's grandmother.

She was the daughter of Carl Dolphus Pelston and Mary Pearl Branham of Cumberland County, Kentucky. Proven That parentage is carried three ways at once: by Brent's direct family knowledge (his ruling of 16 October 2026: "they are her parents — we knew her, she knew them — but don't have the paper trail"); by DNA, because Barbara Price's AncestryDNA kit shares 387 cM with Misti Pelston with Carl and Mary Pearl as the common ancestors, which Mary could not carry unless she was Carl's daughter; and by paper, because her sister Vernie Lee's 1934 Kentucky marriage register names the bride's parents outright as "C. D. Pelston and Pearl Branham Pelston." What is missing is only the paper that names Mary herself — her Kentucky birth certificate, a $10 document the family has approved ordering. It now papers a known fact; it no longer decides one.

Brent himself shares 1,710 cM with Mary — squarely in the grandparent range. Proven The relationship this page is anchored on was never the question. The questions are in the details of the life, and they are worked below.

§2 Kentucky beginnings

Mary was born 1 March 1926 in Burkesville, Cumberland County, Kentucky. The date is proven; the town is the family's and the trees' consistent word; the county is proven by the Kentucky Birth Index. Her civil birth certificate has not yet been pulled — the one documentary gap at the very start of her life.

Her birth date, 1 March 1926, is proven by the Kentucky Birth Index entry for Cumberland County, by her age of 88 in her 2014 obituary, and by her Indiana death certificate (No. 019113), which repeats it. Proven The place is graded one step lower: the index proves Cumberland County, and "Burkesville" — the county seat, and the place every tree and the family give — is probable until the certificate itself is read. Probable

She grew up in a full house. The 1930 census (worked in §3) shows Carl and Pearl's children in order: Euel, 13; Vernie Lee, 10; Clyde, 8; James, 6; Mary herself, 4, written down as "Euylene"; and the baby Burneice — Bernice — not yet a year old. Vernie Lee married at fifteen, in June 1934, to Queen England, with her father standing surety on the bond; that register is the paper that names Mary's parents. Proven Later, half-brothers and half-sisters would come through Carl's second family with Elsie — Walter and Larry Pelston among them, whom Mary's own obituary names fondly as her brothers. Their full placement belongs to Carl's second family's story, held in the lane; what matters here is that Mary counted them as brothers, and the obituaries on both sides agree she was their sister. Proven as half-brothers (Carl × Elsie), "sister" in her obituary being the family's loose and warmer word.

The third woman in the farmyard photograph. The family filename calls her "Pearl," a fourth sister. But the family's own picture register, in another entry for this same grouping, writes it out: "Brenice, Mary, Pearl (mom), and Vernie Lee Pelston" — Pearl labeled mom: Mary Pearl Branham, the sisters' mother. The woman third from left looks older than the other three, and no record anywhere reviewed in this lane shows Carl and Pearl having a daughter named Pearl.

The fuller scan of this photograph carries the surname in its filename — Bernice-Mary-Pearl-Branham-VernieLee — which points the same way: the third woman is the mother, a Branham, standing with three of her daughters. The research lane's working verdict is that she is the mother. Probable But no document names the sitter, so on this page the question stays where the evidence leaves it: Open — a sister called Pearl, or their mother Pearl Branham. The page prints both readings rather than choosing in the caption what the records have not chosen.

The Kentucky household did not hold. Carl and Pearl divorced in the 1930s — the fact is plain from the 1940 census, which finds Carl, 49, marked divorced, living back under his parents' roof, while Mary is living somewhere else entirely (§3). Probable The divorce record itself has never been found: Kentucky's divorce index starts in 1962, and eight targeted newspaper searches for a 1930s filing came back silent. Open Mary's mother later married Jimmie Wooton — by 1950 the census finds Jimmy and Pearl Wooten, she aged 54, farming at Gradyville in Adair County, with Mary's sister Bernice, 20 and never married, as their stepdaughter in the house. Mary Pearl died in 1983 as Mary Pearl Wooten. Probable — her own death certificate, which would name her parents and settle several questions at once, is the lane's standing decider and has not yet been pulled.

§3 The census trail

Three census sheets catch Mary across twenty years: a four-year-old in her father's house, a fourteen-year-old stepdaughter in another man's house, and a twenty-four-year-old separated mother heading her own household in Chicago. Each sheet spells her name a different way. Walk them one at a time.

1930 — "Euylene," age 4, in Carl and Pearl's house

Cumberland County, Kentucky · District 2 · ED 29-4 · Dwelling 233 · Read from the sheet image, 26 September 2026
HeadCarl Pelston, 39 — indexed as "Carl O." — married at 25
WifePearl, 34 — married at 20
ChildrenEuel, 13 · Vernie E., 10 · Clyde, 8 · James, 6 · "Euylene," 4 · Burneice, 0
The identification"Euylene," 4, in this household, is Mary Eveline — the age is exact for a girl born 1 March 1926, the name is the enumerator's ear-spelling of Eveline, and she sits in the right place in the birth order. Probable — a tight chain, but no vital record yet welds the census child to the woman; her birth certificate is the weld.
The neighborsNot yet read off this sheet. The lane's standing rule is that the households on either side of a subject's get read and recorded; for 1930 that chore is still outstanding, and the page leaves it honestly on the list rather than guessing names. Open

This is the last sheet that shows Mary's family whole: father, mother, and six children under one Cumberland County roof. Within the decade the marriage had ended, and the next census scatters them.

1940 — "Evelyn Pelston," 14, stepdaughter

Cumberland County, Kentucky · ED 29-4 · Sheet 5-A · Enumerated 9 April 1940 by George Henry Bowick · Re-read at image grade, 15 October 2026
HeadJames Wooton, 27 — farmer, renting a farm home at $1 a month; the sheet's formal "James," the family's "Jimmie"
WifePearl Wooton, 31
Stepchildren"Evelyn Pelston," 14 — "Stp Daughter" · "Nice" Pelston, 10 — "Stp Daughter" (Bernice, by the resolved name chain Burneice → Nice → Bernice) · James R. Pelston, 6 — "Stp Son"
Above themVisited No. 75: Robert Gibson, 69, farmer, and his wife Ellie, 64 — no kin surnames
Below themVisited No. 77: Robert Baker, 43, farmer, and his wife Lucy, 40 — no kin surnames. No Pelston, Branham, or Wooton appears in either neighboring house; the only Pelstons on this stretch of the sheet are the three stepchildren.

Two things about this sheet were argued over for years, and both are now settled as far as the sheet itself can settle them. First, the relationship word: two earlier readings of Mary's entry conflicted — "Stp Daughter" against plain "Daughter." The high-resolution re-read of 15 October 2026 settles it: the enumerator wrote "Stp Daughter" for all three children, cleanly, with no overwriting. Proven And she was Jimmie Wooton's stepdaughter — never Carl's. The older claim that the 1940 census called her Carl's stepdaughter is disproven; Carl is on another sheet the same spring, divorced and living with his parents. Disproven Brent's own family statement, given the same evening, says it in five words: "Wooten is step dad. See prior census."

Second, the wife. The Pearl in this house, 31, is not Mary's mother. She is a younger Pearl — born about 1909–10, daughter of a "Joe Pelston" and a "Sissie (or Lissie) Pelston" per the register of her marriage to Jimmie Wooton at Columbia on 9 July 1937 — while Mary Pearl Branham, born 1897, became Jimmie's wife only later, by 1950. That is the lane's two-Pearls finding (26 September 2026), and it explains the household: Mary's mother had gone, a younger kinswoman-Pearl kept the house, and Mary and her little sister and brother lived there as the stepchildren. Probable — the ages, the 1937 register's parent names, and the 1950 sheet all line up, but the one document that would close it, the death certificate of Pearl Wooten, has not been pulled. What the arrangement means for Mary is plain enough without it: at fourteen she was a stepdaughter in a rented farmhouse, her parents' marriage over, Kentucky nearly done with her.

1950 — "Mary E" Dedo, 24, separated, heading her own house

Chicago, Cook County, Illinois · ED 103-1399 · Page 12 · Read on the National Archives' 1950 census site, 23 September 2026
Head"Mary E" Dedo, 24 — marital status "Sep" (separated) — born Kentucky
DaughterBarbara S., 4 — born Illinois
LodgersMaxine Rowe, 18, of Kentucky, bench assembly · Charlotte D., of Illinois
Her work"Bench assembly," 40 hours a week, in a manufacturing industry — the census names the trade, never the employer
GradeRead on the Archives' site and transcribed in the lane; the sheet image itself was not banked locally. Probable

Ten years and four hundred miles from the Wooton farmhouse: Mary is a head of household in Chicago, a separated mother of a four-year-old, working a factory bench forty hours a week and taking in lodgers. Her first marriage is over in everything but the paperwork — the census says "separated," and no divorce decree has ever been found (§6). Within the year she would marry again.

Between the sheets there are gaps the censuses cannot fill: no record yet found fixes when Mary left Kentucky, and the state-level traces of her Chicago forties come from the marriage license and the 1950 sheet alone. Those gaps stand as gaps in the ledger below.

§4 Chicago, and the Western Electric story

By the summer of 1944 Mary was in Chicago and about to be married. How she got there, and where she worked, the records mostly do not say. What they do not say, she did — to her grandson, in her own words.

Her own telling, as Brent carries it: Mary met Edward Dedo when both of them worked at Western Electric — the Hawthorne Works in Cicero, the vast telephone-equipment plant that employed half the near-west suburbs. She told her grandson so herself.

That is graded exactly as what it is: her telling — cherished family knowledge from the woman herself, and unprovable by any paper this lane holds. Open as a documentary fact. The 1944 marriage license lists no occupations. The Hawthorne Works' personnel files have never been found to search. What can be said is that the one employment record Mary does have — the 1950 census's "bench assembly," forty hours a week in manufacturing — is precisely the kind of work Western Electric's benches did, and the plant sat a short ride from where she lived and married. Consistent is not confirmed, and this page keeps the two words separate: the story stands as she told it, marked as a telling.

The timing of her move north is likewise unrecorded. She is in Cumberland County in April 1940, a stepdaughter of fourteen; she is in Chicago by 27 July 1944, when Cook County issued her marriage license. Somewhere in those four years — wartime years, when the Hawthorne Works was hiring by the thousand — a Kentucky girl made the road north that her whole generation of Cumberland County was making. The records in hand do not date the trip, and the page does not invent a date for it. Open

§5 The wedding — 5 August 1944

On Saturday, 5 August 1944, Mary Pelston, 18, married Edward Joseph Dedo, 26, at St. Camillus Church, Chicago. The license survives as an image and has been read digit by digit; the studio portraits survive in two prints. This is the best-documented day of her young life.

LicenseNo. 1522327, Cook County — issued 27 July 1944 by the image's own date; an Ancestry index says 24 July. The image is followed here, the mismatch left standing. Open
Ceremony5 August 1944, St. Camillus Church, Chicago (55th & Lockwood); returned and filed 7 August 1944
AgesEdward 26 · Mary 18
OfficiantA Roman Catholic priest of the parish; the signature has been read two ways ("Macey" / Madaj, the parish's first assistant of those years) and stays unread to certainty. Open

Shirley Sleiva. One name rides at the edge of this wedding and has never been explained. Copies of Mary's portrait traveled under the filename "Mary Meier at Shirley Sleiva's Wedding" — the mislabeling that hid the portrait's true occasion for years. Brent's word (19 October 2026) is that Shirley was a friend of Mary's. Whether she stood as an attendant on 5 August 1944, or lent her name to the prints some other way, no record in the lane says. She stands here as she stands in the file: a friend, at the edge of the wedding story, unexplained. Open

§6 Two households

The Dedo marriage gave Mary her first child and ended within six years. The Meier marriage, made in November 1950, lasted fifty-eight. Between the two stands a paperwork gap this file has never closed.

Her daughter Barbara Sue Dedo was born 4 June 1945 — Brent's mother. Proven (the 1950 census's "Barbara S., 4"; both parents' obituaries; the family itself). The open-field photograph below catches the young family whole, about 1948: Edward in his hat, Mary laughing, Barbara in a bonnet between them, already walking.

By April 1950 the marriage was finished in fact: the census calls Mary "separated," and Edward's own death certificate, decades later, lists him as divorced. Probable But the divorce decree itself — the Cook County record that would date the ending — has never been found. There is no free index to 1940s Cook County divorces, and the search stands where it stood: inferred, not documented. Open It is an open item this page shares with Edward's: his page carries the same gap from the other side of the marriage.

On 11 November 1950 Mary married Warren H. Meier in Cook County — license No. 2157987, issued 27 October 1950. Probable The date and the license number come from index entries and the trees; the license image itself has not yet been read, which is why this marriage is graded one step below the first. (An earlier profile gave the wedding date as 27 October 1950 — that is the license's issue date wearing the wedding's clothes.) Warren was a Cicero-born Army Air Force veteran of the Second World War, a decade into his life when Mary met him; the "H." is all the records give for his middle initial — "Henry," seen on some profiles, is unsourced and is not used here. Open

Two children came of the Meier marriage: Debra Lynn Meier, born 11 December 1954 in Berwyn — Brent's aunt Deb — and Tim William Meier, born 2 October 1959 in Chicago, at whose Indiana home Mary would die fifty-five years later. Probable (both parents' obituaries; Tim's own 2025 obituary names the sibling group entire: "older sisters Barb (Ken) Price and Deb (Bill) Dykema").

§7 North Riverside — the grandmother I knew

In 1952 the Meiers bought a house new: 8912 W. 24th Street, North Riverside, from the Achilles Homes development, at $15,950. Mary lived in that house's orbit for the rest of her life. It is the house her grandchildren knew her in.

The address is graded probable, not proven: it rests on address histories for both Mary and Warren, on a modern photograph of the house whose plaque reads 8912 (an earlier reading of "1013" was a misread, since corrected), and on a 1952 newspaper advertisement for the development — the family files it as "Ma and Pa's house," Ma and Pa being Warren and Mary. Probable North Riverside and Berwyn run together in her records — the funeral homes, the church, the obituaries' datelines — the near-west-suburban world she had come to as a bride in 1944 and never left again.

This is the stretch of her life the documents say least about and the family knows most about, and the page does not pretend otherwise. The censuses end in 1950. What fills the next six decades in the file is the texture of a known grandmother: the house on 24th Street, Warren beside her, Barbara and Deb and Tim grown, grandchildren and then eighteen great-grandchildren arriving in the obituary's arithmetic. Brent's book of her — The Grandmother I Knew, the storybook this page stands beside — carries those memories in full; the page's work is to keep the record straight underneath them.

Warren died 14 December 2008, age 88, of North Riverside, formerly of Berwyn; his Chicago Tribune obituary names him "beloved husband of Mary, nee Pelston," a veteran of the Army Air Force, buried from Kuratko-Nosek Funeral Home with a funeral at Oak Park Avenue Baptist Church in Berwyn, interment at Mount Emblem Cemetery. Proven Mary was his widow for the last five and a half years of her life.

§8 The last years

Mary Eveline Pelston Meier died on 22 April 2014, aged 88, at her son Tim's home in Atlanta, Hamilton County, Indiana. Proven — Indiana death certificate No. 019113 names her, gives the birth date and place this page opens with, and names her parents, Carl Pelston and Pearl Branham. (An earlier tree entry put her death in North Riverside; that was the funeral-home town mistaken for the place of death, and it is corrected wherever this file controls the text.) Her residence to the end was North Riverside; she died, as the old often do, under a child's roof.

The visitation was Saturday, 26 April 2014, at Joseph Nosek & Sons Funeral Home, 6716 W. 16th Street, Berwyn, with the chapel service at one o'clock and interment at Mt. Emblem Cemetery, 520 E. Grand Avenue, Elmhurst — the same ground where Warren lay. Probable as a burial record: the interment rests on the obituary's direction and the memorial record; Mt. Emblem's own interment entry has been requested in the lane's list and not yet read.

What stands proved of Mary Pelston needs no embroidery: a Kentucky girl of Cumberland County, a stepdaughter at fourteen, a Chicago bride at eighteen, a separated factory-bench mother at twenty-four, and then sixty years a North Riverside wife, mother, and grandmother, dead at eighty-eight among her children. The gaps in her paper — a birth certificate unordered, a divorce decree unfound, a second license unread — are named on this page as gaps, because she deserves the same honesty her grandson gives the strangers in this file. She was known. The records are still catching up to what the family already knew.

§11 Open questions

What this page leaves open, on purpose, until a record closes it.

  1. Her Kentucky birth certificate — the $10 documentary completion, approved in principle. It would paper her birth date, town, and parentage at vital-record grade. Until it is read, Burkesville stays probable.
  2. The third woman in the farmyard photograph — a sister called Pearl, or the mother, Pearl Branham? The lane leans mother; nothing names the sitter. A dated, captioned print or a direct family identification would close it.
  3. Pearl Wooton's death certificate — the standing decider for the two-Pearls question: its parent names and birth date settle outright which Pearl was Jimmie's wife in which years.
  4. The Dedo divorce decree — Cook County, sometime 1944–1950. No free index exists; the decree's date and grounds are unknown. Shared with Edward's page.
  5. The 1950 Meier license image — the index gives license 2157987, issued 27 Oct 1950, wedding 11 Nov 1950. Reading the image would lift the second marriage to proven and settle the "Meyers vs Meier" spelling that three Kentucky sibling obituaries carry.
  6. Shirley Sleiva — Mary's friend; her tie to the wedding day itself is unexplained.
  7. Florence or Mary, left or right — the positions in the c. 1945 trio photograph remain tentative and unconfirmed.
  8. Western Electric — her telling stands; no personnel record has been found to test it, and none may survive.
  9. The 1930 neighbors — the households beside Carl and Pearl's in Dwelling 233's neighborhood have not yet been read off the sheet.
  10. The late-life portrait — its date, occasion, and possible memorial use are unproven.
  11. Mt. Emblem's interment record — requested in the lane's list; the cemetery's own entry would lift her burial to proven.
